steps.explanationAfterStep: The primary alcohol and tert-butanol have similar acidity, so a catalytic amount of tert-butoxide keeps a little alkoxide present throughout.

An intramolecular oxa-Michael addition: 5-exo-trig (a five-membered ring; the C=C π bond that breaks is outside the ring; the carbon attacked is trigonal). The chain lets the oxygen approach the alkene carbon from above the plane, at the Bürgi–Dunitz angle of about 107°, so Baldwin's rules allow it.
Protonating the enolate on carbon gives the ketone and returns tert-butoxide, so the base is only needed in catalytic amount.

title: Ring closure by oxa-Michael addition
subtitle: An alkoxide adds to an enone in its own chain: 5-exo-trig, allowed by Baldwin
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 31 (Saturated heterocycles and stereoelectronics)
Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 22 (Conjugate addition and nucleophilic aromatic substitution)

enolate.caption: the enolate, now carrying a tetrahydrofuran ring + tert-butanol
hintTiers: The enolate is a strong base. Which carbon gives the ketone back when it is protonated?
The C=C π pair takes the O–H proton of tert-butanol on the α-carbon, and the oxygen lone pair re-forms the C=O. Three arrows.
Enolate oxygen lone pair → C=O π bond; C=C π bond → new C–H bond from the α-carbon to the hydrogen of tert-butanol; that O–H bond → lone pair on its oxygen.
enolate.learnerPrompt: The enolate takes a proton back from tert-butanol.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Ring opening (retro-Michael) does happen, but it is the way back. Protonating the enolate gives the stable ketone.
There is no electrophilic carbon here. The enolate acts as a base and takes the O–H proton of tert-butanol.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right so far: the α-carbon takes the proton. Where does the O–H bonding pair of tert-butanol go?
That gives the enol, which would tautomerise to the same ketone. Here, protonate the α-carbon directly.

alkoxide.caption: the alkoxide of the hydroxy enone + tert-butanol
hintTiers: A conjugate (Michael) addition: which carbon of the enone is electrophilic? Then count the ring size.

The alkoxide attacks the β-carbon of the enone (the alkene carbon further from C=O); the C=C π pair moves to make C=C with the carbonyl carbon, and the C=O π pair moves onto oxygen. A five-membered ring forms. Three arrows.
Alkoxide lone pair → new O–C bond to the β-carbon; C=C π bond → a π bond between the α-carbon and the carbonyl carbon; C=O π bond → lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen.
alkoxide.learnerPrompt: The alkoxide meets the enone in its own chain. Close the ring.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The α-carbon is not electrophilic: conjugation puts the positive end of the enone on the β-carbon. (Closing onto it would also be a 6-endo-trig ring.)
Adding to the carbonyl carbon would make a seven-membered ring (7-exo-trig). Baldwin allows it, but seven-membered rings close slowly and the hemiketal falls apart again. The five-membered ring wins.
That takes the proton back from tert-butanol. The alkoxide is ready: use it on the enone.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right so far: the ring has formed and the C=C has moved. The carbonyl carbon now has five bonds: move the C=O π pair.
Right atom. That carbon now has five bonds: move the C=C π pair, and then the C=O π pair.

reactants.caption: (E)-7-hydroxyhept-3-en-2-one + potassium tert-butoxide (catalytic)
hintTiers: The OH must become an alkoxide before it can add. Which base is in the flask?
tert-Butoxide takes the O–H proton; the O–H bonding pair stays on the oxygen of the chain. Two arrows.
tert-Butoxide lone pair → new O–H bond to the alcohol's hydrogen; the alcohol's O–H bond → lone pair on its oxygen.
reactants.learnerPrompt: A hydroxy enone and a catalytic base. First, make the nucleophile.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The neutral alcohol adds only very slowly. The base is there to make the alkoxide: deprotonate first.
tert-Butoxide is a hindered, poor nucleophile, and it is present only in catalytic amount. It is the base here.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: tert-butoxide takes the O–H proton. Where does the O–H bonding pair go?

mechanismSummary: tert-Butoxide removes the O–H proton, and the alkoxide adds to the β-carbon of the enone in the same chain: a conjugate (oxa-Michael) addition that closes a five-membered ring. The enolate formed takes the proton back from tert-butanol on carbon, giving the ketone and regenerating the base. Baldwin calls this closure 5-exo-trig: favoured, because the nucleophile can reach the π* orbital of the alkene at the Bürgi–Dunitz angle (about 107°) from outside the forming ring. A 5-endo-trig closure, with the alkene inside the new ring, cannot reach that angle and is disfavoured.
